concepts.title: Translation Invariance in CNNs

position.section_title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

concepts.one_liner: Convolution is a suitable strategy for images because visual content tends to be translation invariant, meaning objects look the same regardless of their position.
concepts.content: For images, convolution is an especially suitable strategy because visual content tends to be translation invariant, and the convolution operator is also translation invariant. Typically, objects can appear anywhere in an image and look the same. This is because as objects move across the frame, their position changes but their identity and appearance do not. More generally, as a camera pans across a scene, the content shifts in position but is otherwise unchanged. Because the visual world is roughly translation invariant, it is justified to process each patch the same way, regardless of its position or its translation away from some canonical center patch.
concepts.motivation_md: In computer vision, the identity of an object doesn't change just because it moves to a different part of the frame. Recognizing this property allows us to use convolutions to share weights across all spatial locations, drastically reducing the number of parameters needed compared to fully connected networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Visual content is translation invariant because object identity is independent of spatial position.
 - Convolutional operators are mathematically translation invariant, making them ideal for image processing.
 - This property justifies processing every image patch with the same function.

concepts.title: Translation Invariant

position.section_title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

concepts.one_liner: Translation invariant means processing each patch identically using the same function, such that shifting the input results in an equivalent shift in the output.
concepts.content: Translation invariant means we process each patch identically, using the same function $f$. Some texts instead use the term to describe convolutions. This places emphasis on the fact that if we shift the input signal by some translation, then the output signal will get shifted by the same amount. That is, if $f$ is a convolution, we have that property.
concepts.motivation_md: This definition provides a formal mathematical basis for why we can use the same filter across an entire image. It ensures that the features detected are consistent regardless of where they appear in the input.
concepts.recap_md:
- Translation invariance implies using the same function $f$ for every input patch.
 - If an input signal shifts, a translation-invariant output signal shifts by the same amount.
 - Convolutions are a primary example of translation-invariant functions.

concepts.title: Encoder
concepts.one_liner: An encoder is an analysis network that maps data to a typically lower-dimensional representation.
concepts.content: In the context of deep networks, we call the analysis network an encoder. An encoder maps from data to a representation of that data, which is usually lower dimensional. In the context of CNNs, encoders are typically nets that take an image as input and then downsample it, layer by layer, until producing a much lower-dimensional feature map as output.
concepts.motivation_md: Encoders are used to extract the most essential features from raw data, compressing high-dimensional inputs like images into a compact form that captures semantic meaning while discarding noise.
concepts.recap_md:
- An encoder acts as an analysis network mapping data to a representation.
 - The resulting representation is usually lower-dimensional than the input.
 - In CNNs, encoders typically involve downsampling layers to produce feature maps.

key_passage.text: An encoder maps from data to a representation of that data, which is usually lower dimensional, and a decoder performs the inverse operation, mapping from a representation back to the data.

motivation.text: In the context of deep networks, we call the analysis network an encoder and the synthesis network a decoder.

concepts.title: Decoder
concepts.one_liner: A decoder is a synthesis network that maps from a low-dimensional representation back to the original data format.
concepts.content: In the context of deep networks, we call the synthesis network a decoder. A decoder performs the inverse operation of an encoder, mapping from a representation back to the data. It takes a set of low-dimensional features as input, then upsamples them, layer by layer, until producing an image as the final output.
concepts.motivation_md: Decoders are essential for tasks where the output must match the input format, such as image reconstruction, segmentation, or generation, by expanding compressed features back into a full-resolution signal.
concepts.recap_md:
- A decoder is a synthesis network that maps representations back to data.
 - It performs the inverse operation of an encoder.
 - In CNNs, decoders use upsampling layers to generate high-dimensional outputs from low-dimensional features.

concepts.title: Information Bottleneck
concepts.one_liner: An information bottleneck is a low-dimensional representation between an encoder and decoder that forces the network to learn abstract features.
concepts.content: Encoder-decoders introduce an information bottleneck, meaning the representation between the encoder and decoder is low-dimensional and can only transmit so much information. This constraint forces abstraction, requiring the network to compress the signal and retain only the most important features.
concepts.motivation_md: By restricting the amount of information that can pass through the network, we force the model to ignore irrelevant noise and focus on learning the most salient, high-level patterns in the data.
concepts.recap_md:
- The information bottleneck is a low-dimensional state between encoder and decoder.
 - It limits information transmission to force the learning of abstract representations.
 - Compressing the signal in this way provides benefits in memory and compute efficiency.

concepts.title: Skip Connection
concepts.one_liner: A skip connection is an identity pathway that connects two disparate layers of a network to shuttle information directly across blocks.
concepts.content: To circumvent the problem of information loss, we can add pathways that shuttle information directly across blocks of layers in the net. A skip connection $f$ is simply an identity pathway that connects two disparate layers of a net, $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Deep networks often suffer from vanishing gradients or loss of spatial detail. Skip connections allow gradients and original input features to bypass certain layers, making it easier to train very deep architectures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Skip connections shuttle information directly across different layers of a network.
 - They are defined as an identity pathway where $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}$.
 - They help preserve information that might otherwise be lost in deep processing blocks.

concepts.title: U-Net
concepts.one_liner: A U-Net is an encoder-decoder architecture with mirrored skip connections that concatenate activations to preserve high-frequency spatial information.
concepts.content: Adding skip connections to an encoder-decoder results in an architecture known as a U-Net. In this architecture, skip connections are arranged in a mirror pattern, where layer $l$ is connected directly to layer $(L-l)$. The output of a skip connection must somehow be reintegrated into the network; U-nets do this by concatenating the activations from the prior layer to the activations on the later layer, along the channel dimension. This architecture can maintain the information-bottleneck of the encoder-decoder, with its incumbent benefits in terms of memory and compute efficiency and forced abstraction, while also allowing residual information to flow through the skip connections, thereby not sacrificing the ability to output high-frequency spatial predictions. U-Nets look a lot like steerable pyramids, consisting of a downsampling analysis path followed by an upsampling synthesis path, with skip connections in between mirror image stages. The main difference is that the U-Net has learned filters and nonlinearities. (see figure: U-net architecture. Each block contains a series of layers. The skip connections concatenate activations.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard encoder-decoders lose fine-grained spatial details during downsampling. U-Nets solve this by 'shunting' high-resolution features from the encoder directly to the decoder, which is critical for tasks like medical image segmentation.
concepts.recap_md:
- U-Nets use mirrored skip connections to link encoder layers to corresponding decoder layers.
 - Skip connections in U-Nets function by concatenating activations along the channel dimension.
 - This design balances abstract feature learning with the preservation of high-frequency spatial detail.

concepts.title: Residual Network (ResNet)
concepts.one_liner: Residual Networks (ResNets) are deep architectures that use skip connections to add activations from one block to the next.
concepts.content: Another popular architecture that uses skip connections is called Residual Networks or ResNets. ResNets often exploit skip connections by being very deep; for example, they may be hundreds of blocks deep. (see figure: ResNet architecture. Each block contains a series of layers. The skip connections add activations from one block to the next.)
concepts.motivation_md: As networks get deeper, they become harder to train due to the vanishing gradient problem. ResNets allow the network to learn 'residuals' (changes to the input) rather than the full transformation, making extremely deep networks viable.
concepts.recap_md:
- ResNets utilize skip connections to pass information across blocks of layers.
 - Unlike U-Nets which concatenate, ResNets typically add activations from the skip connection to the block output.
 - This architecture enables the training of very deep networks, sometimes hundreds of layers deep.

concepts.title: Multichannel Convolution Notation
concepts.one_liner: Multichannel convolution notation tracks input channels, filter banks, and output dimensions using tensor representations.
concepts.content:
Notation for multichannel convolutions can be complex, so it is helpful to define the specific components. The input signal's $c_{\texttt{1}}$-th channel is denoted as $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[c_{\texttt{1}},:,:]$. The filter bank consists of $C_{\texttt{out}}$ filters, $[\mathbf{w}[:,0,:,:], \ldots, \mathbf{w}[:,C_{\texttt{out}}-1,:,:]]$, where each filter applies a convolutional kernel per input channel and sums the responses. This layer maps inputs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\texttt{in}}\times N \times M}$ to outputs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}\in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\texttt{out}}\times N \times M}$. The entire filter bank is represented by a tensor $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\texttt{in}}\times C_{\texttt{out}}\times K \times K}$, where $K$ is the spatial, square kernel size.

(see figure: Multichannel convolution.)
concepts.motivation_md: As neural networks process data with multiple features (like RGB channels), standard 2D convolution must be extended. This notation provides a formal mathematical framework to track how multiple input channels are transformed into multiple output channels through a bank of 4D weight tensors.
concepts.recap_md: - Input signals are represented as 3D tensors with dimensions for channels, height, and width.

key_passage.text: The filter bank is $C_{\texttt{out}}$ filters, $[\mathbf{w}[:,0,:,:], \ldots, \mathbf{w}[:,C_{\texttt{out}}-1,:,:]]$, each of which applies one convolutional filter per input channel and then sums the responses over all these filters. This convolutional layer maps inputs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\texttt{in}}\times N \times M}$ to outputs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}\in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\texttt{out}}\times N \times M}$. The filter bank is represented by a tensor $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{\texttt{in}}\times C_{\texttt{out}}\times K \times K}$, where $K$ is the (spatial, square) kernel size.

concepts.title: Strided Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Strided convolution reduces output resolution by applying the filter at regular intervals defined by vertical and horizontal strides.
concepts.content:
Convolutional layers typically maintain the spatial resolution of the signal they process. However, it is often sufficient or desirable to output a lower resolution. This is achieved with strided convolution:

$$\begin{aligned}x_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] = b + \sum_{k_1,k_2=-K}^K w[k_1,k_2] x_{\texttt{in}}[s_n n-k_1,s_m m-k_2] \end{aligned}$$

where $s_n$ and $s_m$ are the strides in the vertical and horizontal directions, respectively. Strided convolution effectively subsamples the input during the convolution process.

(see figure: Strided convolution.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard convolutions can be computationally expensive and may preserve more spatial detail than necessary for high-level feature recognition. Striding provides a built-in way to downsample data and increase the receptive field of subsequent layers.
concepts.recap_md: - Strided convolution uses step sizes $s_n$ and $s_m$ to skip input pixels during application.

concepts.title: Dilated Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Dilated convolution spaces out the filter elements rather than the application points to increase the receptive field without losing resolution.
concepts.content:
Dilated convolution is similar to strided convolution but spaces out the filter itself rather than spacing out where the filter is applied to the image:

$$\begin{aligned} x_{\texttt{out}}[n,m] = b + \sum_{k_1,k_2=-K}^K w[k_1,k_2] x_{\texttt{in}}[n-d_kk_1,m-d_kk_2] \end{aligned}$$

concepts.motivation_md: To capture long-range dependencies in an image, one usually needs very large filters or many layers, both of which are expensive. Dilation allows a small filter to 'see' a wider area by skipping pixels within the kernel's footprint.

concepts.title: Cascading Dilated Filters
concepts.one_liner: Cascading dilated filters with increasing dilation rates creates efficient, large-scale kernels capable of capturing diverse spatial frequencies.
concepts.content:
Dilation can be used to increase the family of useful filters. For instance, by composing three convolutions with $d_k=1$, $d_k=2$, and $d_k=4$ together (@fig-convolutional_neural_networks-dilated_conv_cascade), one can create a kernel that can switch during learning between high and low spatial frequencies and small and large kernels.

(see figure: Convolving dilated filters creates a new filter that can measure effects at a mixture of frequencies.)

This results in a kernel with a size of $9 \times 9$ (81 values) defined by only 27 parameters. The relative computational efficiency increases when we cascade more filters with higher levels of dilation. As shown in @fig-convolutional_neural_nets-kernels_resulting_from_dilated_filters, a cascade of three dilated convolutions can generate a large family of filters with different scales, orientations, shifts, and patterns such as corner, long edge, and curved edge detectors.

(see figure: Example kernels that each result from convolving three filters.)

The diversity of kernels one can build is further illustrated by convolving three random $3 \times 3$ kernels sampled from a Gaussian distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Large kernels are needed to detect large-scale structures, but they require many parameters. Cascading dilated filters allows the network to learn complex, wide-reaching patterns using far fewer weights than a standard dense large kernel.

concepts.title: Low-Rank Filters
concepts.one_liner: Low-rank filters use a small number of weights to parameterize large kernels, capturing long-range dependencies efficiently.
concepts.content: Dilation is one way to create a big filter that is parameterized by just a small number of weights; this is known as a low-rank filter. This technique is useful in contexts where it is known that effective filters possess a low-rank structure. Dilation specifically uses this trick to construct large kernels capable of capturing long-range dependencies without the computational cost of a fully parameterized large matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: High-dimensional filters are prone to overfitting and are computationally expensive. Low-rank approximations allow the model to retain the expressive power of large spatial footprints while keeping the parameter count manageable.
concepts.recap_md: - Low-rank filters parameterize large spatial areas with few weights.

concepts.title: Separable Filters
concepts.one_liner: Separable filters are low-rank filters formed by the outer product of two 1D kernels, often implemented as sequential $K \times 1$ and $1 \times K$ layers.
concepts.content:
Separable filters are a type of low-rank filter useful in many applications. A convolutional layer with separable filters can be created by stacking two convolutional layers in sequence: the first with $K \times 1$ kernels and the second with $1 \times K$ kernels. Their composition is equivalent to a single layer with $K \times K$ separable filters. When convolving a row and column vector, $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}^\mathsf{T} \circ \mathbf{v}$, the result is the outer product: $w[n,m] = u[n]v[m]$.

(see figure: Two examples of separable filters.)

While some important kernels are nonseparable, they can often be approximated by a linear combination of a small number of separable filters. For example, the Gaussian Laplacian can be approximated by a separable filter as shown in @fig-convolutional_neural_nets-laplacian_separable_aprox.

(see figure: Approximating a Gaussian Laplacian filter as the outer product of two 1D filters.)
concepts.motivation_md: Convolving with a $K \times K$ filter takes $O(K^2)$ operations, but convolving with two 1D filters takes only $O(K+K)$ operations. Separability significantly reduces the computational burden of image processing and neural networks.

concepts.title: SVD for Filter Decomposition
concepts.one_liner: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) can decompose any $M \times N$ filter into a weighted sum of separable 1D filters.
concepts.content:
Any $M \times N$ filter can be decomposed as a linear sum of $\min(N,M)$ separable filters. These separable filters are obtained by applying the singular value decomposition (SVD) to the kernel array $\mathbf{w}$. The SVD produces three matrices, $\mathbf{U}$, $\mathbf{S}$, and $\mathbf{V}$, such that $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{V}^\mathsf{T}$. The columns of $\mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ represent the separable 1D filters, while the diagonal values of $\mathbf{S}$ serve as linear weights. 

For example, a $3 \times 3$ approximation of a diagonal Gaussian derivative can be written as a sum of two separable Sobel kernels. Computational benefits are primarily realized when using small linear combinations for large kernels. In neural networks, using separable filters allows the model to learn to build complex, nonseparable kernels through combination.
concepts.motivation_md: Not all useful filters are perfectly separable. SVD provides a mathematically grounded way to approximate complex filters using a few separable ones, saving computation while maintaining the desired feature detection properties.

concepts.title: Downsampling Layers
concepts.one_liner: Downsampling layers reduce the spatial dimensions of an input tensor, commonly through strided convolutions or pooling.
concepts.content: Downsampling layers transform an input tensor into an output tensor with smaller spatial dimensions, mapping $\mathbb{R}^{N \times M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N/s_n \times M/s_m}$. One example is strided convolution, which is equivalent to performing a convolution followed by subsampling. Another common type of downsampling layer is pooling.
concepts.motivation_md: As information moves deeper into a network, we want to extract high-level features that are invariant to small shifts. Downsampling reduces the data's spatial size, which lowers computational cost and helps the network focus on 'what' is in the image rather than exactly 'where' it is.

concepts.title: Feature Map Abstraction in Deep Networks
concepts.one_liner: As feature maps go deeper into a network, their spatial resolution decreases while their channels capture increasingly abstract semantic information.
concepts.content: In typical convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the spatial resolution of the feature maps gets lower as we go deeper into the network, and the number of channels increases. Each layer downsamples and adds channels to partially compensate for the reduction in resolution. While on the first layer the feature maps are sensitive to basic patterns in the input image—such as edges and lines—the maps become more abstracted as we go deeper. In image classifier networks, channels in the shallow layers capture basic image features, while channels in the deeper layers increasingly correspond to class semantics (for example, one channel might be a heatmap of where "bird" pixels are).
concepts.motivation_md: This hierarchical structure allows the network to build complex semantic understanding from simple visual primitives. By reducing spatial resolution and increasing channel depth, the network trades precise location information for richer categorical information.
concepts.recap_md:
- Deeper layers exhibit lower spatial resolution and higher channel counts.
 - Shallow layers detect basic patterns like edges and lines.
 - Deep layers represent abstract class semantics and high-level features.

concepts.title: Receptive Fields
concepts.one_liner: The receptive field of a neuron is the specific region of the input signal to which that neuron is sensitive.
concepts.content:
Receptive fields are an important concept when working with CNNs. The receptive field of a neuron is the region of the input signal that the neuron is sensitive to, i.e., its support. In multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), the receptive field of each neuron is the entire input vector since MLPs use fully connected layers. In CNNs, on the other hand, each neuron only sees a portion of the input, since each output neuron on a conv layer is only connected to a subset of inputs to the conv layer, determined by the kernel size of the filter that produces that output.

![Receptive fields in a CNN. The black filled neurons are within the receptive fields of each labeled neuron (left: $x_2[3]$, right: $x_1[5]$).](figures/convolutional_neural_nets/RFs.png){width="100%" #fig-convolutional_neural_networks-RFs}
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding receptive fields is crucial for designing architectures that can capture enough context to make accurate predictions. It defines the 'window' through which a neuron observes the world.
concepts.recap_md:
- A receptive field is the specific input region affecting a neuron's output.
 - In MLPs, neurons have global receptive fields covering the entire input.
 - In CNNs, neurons have local receptive fields determined by kernel size.

concepts.title: Growth of Receptive Fields in CNNs
concepts.one_liner: Receptive fields grow deeper in a network because composing convolutional filters results in a larger equivalent kernel size.
concepts.content: The receptive field grows the deeper we go into the network. To understand why, consider a CNN without nonlinearities. Then the $l+1$-th layer is the composition of $l$ convolutional filters. Composing filters results in a new filter with larger support (kernel size). The same happens in a CNN with pointwise nonlinearities, since pointwise operations do not affect receptive field (the outputs have the same receptive fields as the inputs). Further, whenever we have a downsampling layer by factor $s$, the receptive field of the output is $s$ times larger than the receptive field of the input. Because of these properties, receptive field sizes can grow rapidly as we go deeper in CNNs. Generally, we want the final layer of the CNN to have large enough receptive fields to see the entire input image, so that output neurons are sensitive to all pixels in the input. This can be achieved with a `gap` layer, whose output will always have a receptive field size that covers the entire input.
concepts.motivation_md: For a network to make global decisions (like identifying an object), its final neurons must eventually 'see' the whole image. Understanding how receptive fields grow helps engineers ensure the network has sufficient context.
concepts.recap_md:
- Receptive fields expand as layers are composed, increasing the effective kernel size.
 - Pointwise nonlinearities do not change the size of the receptive field.
 - Downsampling by factor $s$ multiplies the receptive field size by $s$.

concepts.title: Spatial Outputs in CNNs
concepts.one_liner: CNNs can produce spatially varying maps of predictions by maintaining higher resolution and removing global pooling layers.
concepts.content:
To output a spatially varying map of predictions rather than a single probability vector, we can simply downsample less, so that the final layer of the CNN is a feature map that maintains higher spatial resolution. It is also important to remove any global pooling layers. An example of such an architecture is given below:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{z}_1[c_1,:,:] &= \sum_{c=0}^2 \mathbf{w}_1[c,c_1,:,:] \star \mathbf{x} + b_1[c_1]  &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}\\ &&[3 \times N \times M] \rightarrow [C_1 \times N \times M]\nonumber\\ h[c_1,n,m] &= \max(z_1[c_1,n,m],0) &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{relu}\\ &&[C_1 \times N \times M] \rightarrow [C_1 \times N \times M]\nonumber\\ \mathbf{z}_2[c_2,:,:] &= \sum_{c_1=0}^{C_1-1} \mathbf{w}_2[c_1,c_2,:,:] \star \mathbf{x} + b_2[c_2] &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv}\\ &&[C_1 \times N \times M] \rightarrow [C_2 \times N \times M]\nonumber\\ y[k,n,m] &= \frac{e^{-\tau z_2[k,n,m]}}{\sum_{l=1}^K e^{-\tau z_2[l,n,m]}} &\triangleleft \quad \texttt{softmax}\\ &&[K \times N \times M] \rightarrow [K \times N \times M]\nonumber \end{aligned}$$

 - Global pooling layers must be removed to preserve spatial structure.

concepts.title: CNNs as Image-to-Image Architectures
concepts.one_liner: CNNs are best understood as image-to-image architectures that can be applied to any domain where translation is defined.
concepts.content: Although historically CNNs first became popular as image classifiers, this usage hides their real power. Rather than thinking of them as image-to-label architectures, think of them as image-to-image architectures. More generally, CNNs are $\mathcal{X}$-to-$\mathcal{X}$ architectures for any domain $\mathcal{X}$ over which translation can be defined.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing CNNs as image-to-image transforms broadens their application from simple classification to complex tasks like style transfer, denoising, and medical imaging analysis.
concepts.recap_md:
- CNNs are fundamentally image-to-image (or signal-to-signal) architectures.
 - They apply to any domain where translation can be defined.
 - Classification is just a specific use case that reduces the image to a label.

concepts.title: Fully Convolutional Network (FCN)
concepts.one_liner: A fully convolutional network (FCN) is a CNN consisting only of convolutional layers interleaved with pointwise nonlinearities.
concepts.content: The core of CNNs are the convolutional layers. A CNN with only `conv` layers interleaved with pointwise nonlinearities is sometimes called a fully convolutional network or FCN. An FCN functions as a sliding image filter.
concepts.motivation_md: FCNs allow for inputs of arbitrary size and produce spatial outputs, making them ideal for tasks like semantic segmentation where every pixel needs a label.
concepts.recap_md:

 - They act as a single, complex sliding image filter.
 - They avoid fully connected layers that require fixed input sizes.

concepts.title: CNN as a Sliding Filter
concepts.one_liner: A complete CNN composed of convolutional layers and pointwise nonlinearities acts as a nonlinear sliding filter applied identically to every input patch.
concepts.content:
A CNN that processes a signal and outputs a feature map $\mathbf{x}_L$ acts as a sliding filter. The feature vector at any location $i$ is a function $F$ of the input patch in its receptive field: $\mathbf{x}_L[:,i] = F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[:,\texttt{RF}(i)])$. The feature vector at a different pixel $j$ is produced by the same function $F$ applied to a different patch: $\mathbf{x}_L[:,j] = F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[:,\texttt{RF}(j)])$.

(see figure: A CNN is a non-linear filter. Edge colors indicate shared weights; two edges with the same color have the same weight. The colors demonstrate that the same function $F$ is applied to each patch of...)

Without pointwise nonlinearities, the entire CNN is just the composition of a sequence of convolutions, which is itself a convolution. This system processes each input patch independently and identically. Adding pointwise nonlinearities does not change this property because they introduce no interaction between neurons or pixels. Hence, a complete CNN made up only of convolutional layers and pointwise nonlinearities is a nonlinear operator that applies the same transformation independently and identically to each patch of the input signal—a nonlinear filter.
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective explains why CNNs are so efficient and effective for vision: they reuse the same learned features across the entire image, exploiting the fact that a feature (like a wheel or an eye) is meaningful regardless of its location.
concepts.recap_md:
- A CNN applies the same function $F$ to every patch of the input signal.
 - Composing convolutions results in a single equivalent (but larger) convolution.
 - Pointwise nonlinearities preserve the independent processing of input patches.

concepts.title: Locality in Vision

position.section_title: Why Process Images Patch by Patch?

concepts.one_liner: Locality in vision refers to the property where related features clump together in small patches, allowing complex images to be processed as independent pieces.
concepts.content: Treating patches as independent is a divide-and-conquer strategy. A CNN splits a big problem (interpreting a whole photo) into a bunch of smaller problems (interpreting each small patch). This is a good strategy because small problems are easier to solve, can be solved in parallel, and the approach is agnostic to signal length—allowing one to solve arbitrarily large problems by breaking them down. Chopping an image into small patches is sufficient for many vision problems because the world exhibits locality: related things clump together within a single patch, while far apart things can often be safely assumed to be independent.
concepts.motivation_md: Locality is the physical justification for using convolutions. Because pixels are usually only related to their neighbors, we can save immense computational power by focusing on local patches rather than global connections.

 - CNNs exploit locality by treating image patches as independent problems.
 - This approach enables parallel processing and handles variable input sizes.

concepts.title: Convolutional Neural Nets
concepts.one_liner: Convolutional neural nets are architectures specifically designed to exploit the spatial structure inherent in visual signals.
concepts.content: Convolutional neural nets, also called convnets or CNNs, are a neural net architecture especially suited to the structure in visual signals. While standard neural nets are designed to process generic data, CNNs are designed to exploit the special structure found in many domains, particularly visual signals.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard neural networks do not inherently account for the spatial relationships in images. CNNs solve this by using architectures that specifically leverage local patterns and spatial hierarchies.

concepts.title: CNNs as Patch Processing
concepts.one_liner: CNNs function by processing small patches of an input image independently and identically using a scanning neural network.
concepts.content: The key idea of CNNs is to chop up the input image into little patches and then process each patch independently and identically: [FIGURE:bf2d851dfcb790e1]. CNNs are well suited to processing spatial or temporal signals, such as geospatial data or sounds, where there is a natural way to scan across a signal and process each windowed region separately. Each patch is processed with a classifier module, which is a neural net that scans across the input and classifies each patch. If these predictions are rearranged back into the shape of the input image and color coded, they form an input-output mapping: [FIGURE:18506f1d2dfb020b].
concepts.motivation_md: Processing an entire image at once is computationally expensive and ignores local features. Patch-based processing allows the network to learn features that are valid regardless of their location in the image.
concepts.recap_md: - CNNs treat images as a collection of small patches processed by the same neural network module. - The output of this process is a grid of predictions corresponding to the patches in the input. - This scanning mechanism allows CNNs to handle various signal types, including audio and geospatial data.

concepts.title: Semantic Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning a specific class label to every individual pixel in an image.
concepts.content: Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning a class label to each pixel in an image. This can be achieved by chopping up the image into overlapping patches. If done densely, such that each patch is one pixel offset from the last, it produces a full resolution image of predictions: [FIGURE:bc57f84e5eede7f0]. One reason CNNs are powerful is because they can map an input image to an output image with the same shape, rather than outputting a single label.
concepts.motivation_md: Many vision tasks require knowing exactly where objects are and what every pixel represents, rather than just identifying if an object exists anywhere in the image.
concepts.recap_md: - Semantic segmentation produces a label for every pixel, resulting in a dense map of classifications. - CNNs facilitate this by outputting data that maintains the spatial dimensions of the input image.

concepts.title: Feature Map
concepts.one_liner: A feature map is a channel in a neural network's output that highlights specific features, such as edges, found in the input.
concepts.content: Each channel in a convolutional layer is called a feature map, as it shows specific features of the input, such as the location of vertical edges.

concepts.title: Residual Block
concepts.one_liner: A residual block is a neural network component where a skip connection adds the input directly to the output of a block of layers.
concepts.content: In the context of ResNets, skip connections are called residual connections. This kind of skip connection is added to the output of a block of layers $F$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{residual block} \end{aligned}$$ In a residual block, you can think of $F$ as a residual that additively perturbs $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$ to transform it into an improved $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$. If $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ does not have the same dimensionality as $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$, then a linear mapping can be added to convert the dimensions: $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}= F(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}) + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Residual blocks allow for training much deeper networks by making it easier for layers to learn identity mappings, which helps mitigate the vanishing gradient problem and simplifies optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - Residual connections add the input of a block to its output to create a residual mapping.

concepts.title: Ubiquity of CNN Principles
concepts.one_liner: The core principles of CNNs, such as local processing and global information integration, are ubiquitous across many modern architectures like transformers.
concepts.content: While architectures like transformers may appear to replace CNNs in vision problems, the underlying principles of CNNs remain ubiquitous in sensory processing. Transformers also include stages that process each patch identically and independently, but they interleave these stages with other stages that globalize information across patches. Whether these newer architectures are called convolutional is a matter of debate; however, learning the principles allows one to recognize them in all systems regardless of their names.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the fundamental principles of CNNs is more important than the specific architecture, as these concepts of local and global processing reappear in many state-of-the-art models.
concepts.recap_md: - CNN principles like independent patch processing are found in diverse architectures including transformers.

concepts.title: Upsampling Layers
concepts.one_liner: Upsampling layers perform the opposite transformation of downsampling, outputting a tensor that is larger in the spatial dimensions than the input.
concepts.content: Upsampling layers perform the opposite transformation of downsampling, outputting a tensor that is larger in the spatial dimensions than the input: $\mathbb{R}^{N \times M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{Ns_n \times Ms_m}$. One kind of upsampling layer can be made as the analogue of strided convolution. While strided convolution convolves then subsamples, this upsampling layer instead dilates the signal then convolves. Starting with a blank image of zeros, $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$, we set: $$\begin{aligned} h[ns_n, ms_m] &= x_{\texttt{in}}[n, m] & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{dilation}\\ \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{w} \star \mathbf{h} + b & \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{conv} \end{aligned}$$ This equation applies for all integer values of $n \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$ and $m \in \{1,\ldots,M\}$. Sometimes the combination of these two layers is called an UpConv layer or a deconvolution layer (though deconvolution has a different meaning in signal processing).
concepts.motivation_md: Upsampling is necessary for tasks where the output must have a higher resolution than the intermediate feature maps, such as in image synthesis, super-resolution, or semantic segmentation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Upsampling layers increase the spatial dimensions of an input tensor.
 - One common implementation involves dilating the input with zeros followed by a standard convolution.
 - These layers are often referred to as UpConv or deconvolution layers.

concepts.title: Pooling Layers
concepts.one_liner: Pooling layers are downsampling layers that summarize the information in a patch using some aggregate statistic.
concepts.content: Pooling layers are downsampling layers that summarize the information in a patch using some aggregate statistic, such as the patch's mean value (mean pooling) or its max value (max pooling), defined as follows: $$\begin{aligned} x_{\texttt{out}}[i]= \max_{i \in \mathcal{N}(i)} x_{\texttt{in}}[i]& \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{max pooling}\\ x_{\texttt{out}}[i]= \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}(i)} x_{\texttt{in}}[i]& \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \texttt{mean_pooling} \end{aligned}$$ The $\mathcal{N}(i)$ indicates the set of indices in the same patch as index $i$.
concepts.motivation_md: Pooling layers reduce the spatial resolution of feature maps, which decreases computational cost and helps the network focus on the most important features while providing local translation invariance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pooling layers summarize local patches of data into a single representative value.
 - Max pooling selects the maximum value in a neighborhood, while mean pooling calculates the average.
 - These layers effectively downsample the input to reduce dimensionality.

concepts.title: Pooling for Invariance
concepts.one_liner: Pooling converts the equivariance of convolutional layers into invariance by coarsening the response map.
concepts.content: Like all downsampling layers, pooling layers can be used to reduce the resolution of the input tensor, removing high-frequency information in the signal. Pooling is also particularly useful as a way to achieve invariance. Convolutional layers produce outputs that are equivariant to translations of their input; pooling is a way to convert this equivariance into invariance. For example, if a convolutional filter detects vertical edges, max pooling across the resulting response map will coarsen it, yielding a large response anywhere near where the edge was located. If the pooling neighborhood $\mathcal{N}$ is large enough, the output becomes invariant to the exact location of the edge in the input image.
concepts.motivation_md: Invariance is crucial for robust pattern recognition, allowing a network to detect a feature regardless of small shifts in its spatial position.
concepts.recap_md:
- Pooling helps achieve translation invariance by summarizing local neighborhoods.
 - It converts the equivariance of convolutional layers into a representation less sensitive to exact feature locations.
 - Larger pooling neighborhoods provide greater degrees of spatial invariance.

If we use a max pooling filter with large enough neighborhood, the output will be invariant to the location of the edge in the input image.

concepts.title: Channelwise Pooling
concepts.one_liner: Pooling across channels can achieve invariance to transformations like rotation by aggregating responses from filters with different orientations.
concepts.content: Pooling can also be performed across channels to achieve additional kinds of invariance. For example, if a convolutional layer applies a filter bank where each filter looks for edges at a different orientation, max pooling across these channels will result in a feature map that is large wherever an edge of any orientation is found. This logic applies to more complicated patterns as well: by running a bank of filters that look for a pattern at $k$ different orientations and pooling across those channels, a CNN can recognize objects regardless of their rotation. While this strategy can be hand-defined, it is also a strategy that a CNN can learn to use if provided with channelwise pooling layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard spatial pooling provides translation invariance; channelwise pooling extends this to other transformations, such as rotation, by aggregating responses from filters specialized for different variations of the same pattern.
concepts.recap_md:
- Channelwise pooling aggregates information across different feature maps rather than spatial locations.
 - It can be used to make a network invariant to transformations like rotation.
 - This technique allows the network to detect a pattern regardless of which specific oriented filter it activates.

concepts.title: Global Pooling Layers
concepts.one_liner: Global pooling maps a $C \times M \times N$ tensor into a vector of length $C$ by pooling over the entire spatial extent of the feature map.
concepts.content: Global pooling is an extreme form of pooling that operates over the entire spatial extent of a feature map. It is a function that maps a $C \times M \times N$ tensor into a vector of length $C$, where $C$ is the number of channels in the input. Global pooling is generally used in layers very close to the output and can be implemented as global average pooling or global max pooling. While it removes spatial information from each channel, spatial information about input features might still be available within the output vector if different channels learn to be sensitive to features at different spatial positions.
concepts.motivation_md: Global pooling is used to transition from spatial feature maps to a fixed-size vector representation, which is necessary for final classification layers while reducing the number of parameters compared to fully connected layers.
concepts.recap_md:
- Global pooling reduces each spatial feature map to a single scalar value.
 - It is commonly used near the end of a network to produce a feature vector of length equal to the number of channels.
 - Common variants include global average pooling and global max pooling.

concepts.title: Local Normalization Layers
concepts.one_liner: Local normalization layers normalize each activation in a feature map based on the statistics of adjacent activations within a neighborhood.
concepts.content: Local normalization layers are nonlinear filters that normalize each activation in a feature map by statistics of the adjacent activations within some neighborhood. There are many choices for the type of normalization (such as $L_1$ norm, $L_2$ norm, or standardization) and the shape of the neighborhood (such as a square spatial patch or a set of channels). One historically important example is the local response normalization (LRN) filter, which normalizes each activation by the sum of squares of the activations in a window of adjacent channels: $$\begin{aligned} x_{\texttt{out}}[c,n,m] = x_{\texttt{in}}[c,n,m] / \left( \gamma + \alpha \sum_{i=\max(1,c-l)}^{\max(C,c+l)} x_{\texttt{in}}[i,n,m]^2 \right) ^\beta \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\texttt{LRN} \end{aligned}$$ where $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, and $l$ are hyperparameters of the layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Local normalization layers were designed to encourage "lateral inhibition," where high-intensity activations suppress their neighbors, helping the network focus on the most salient features and improving generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Local normalization scales activations based on the values of their neighbors.
 - Local Response Normalization (LRN) specifically normalizes across a window of adjacent channels.
 - These layers use hyperparameters like $\alpha, \beta, \gamma,$ and $l$ to control the normalization effect.

concepts.title: Fully Connected Layer
concepts.one_liner: A fully connected layer is a linear layer where every output neuron is connected to every input neuron.
concepts.content: A fully connected layer (often abbreviated as `fc`) is another name for a linear layer that is full rank. In this architecture, every output neuron is connected to every input neuron, and the mapping is described by a $K \times C$ matrix plus a bias term.
concepts.motivation_md: Fully connected layers allow the network to learn global combinations of features extracted by previous layers, typically serving as the final decision-making component of a classifier.
concepts.recap_md:
- In a fully connected layer, every input unit contributes to every output unit.
 - It is mathematically represented as a matrix multiplication plus a bias.
 - These layers are also known as linear layers.

concepts.title: Adversarial Examples
concepts.one_liner: Adversarial examples are inputs specifically designed to cause a neural network to produce an incorrect output, often through minimal perturbations.
concepts.content: Adversarial examples are test inputs designed to identify weaknesses in a learned representation and training set. One can fool a classifier by creating inputs that look correct to humans but contain specific textures or spectral content that trigger the wrong detectors. For example, multiplying an image by a sinusoidal wave can shift its spectral content to overlap with a different detector, leading to incorrect classification. For complex architectures, adversarial examples are typically obtained as an optimization problem to find the minimal perturbation of an input that will produce the wrong output in the network.
concepts.motivation_md: Studying adversarial examples helps researchers understand the limitations and biases of neural networks, leading to more robust architectures and training methods like adversarial training.
concepts.recap_md:
- Adversarial examples are inputs engineered to trick a model into making a mistake.
 - They often involve small, calculated perturbations that do not change the human perception of the input.
 - Finding these examples is often framed as an optimization problem to find the smallest effective change.

key_passage.text: For complex architectures, adversarial examples are obtained as an optimization problem: What is the minimal perturbation of an input that will produce the wrong output in the network?

question.text: Can we produce test examples that to us look right but for which the network produces the wrong classification output?

motivation.text: The goal of this analysis is to identify weaknesses in the learned representation and in our training set (missing training examples, biases in our data, limitations of the architecture, etc.).

prereq.rationale: Patch processing describes the specific mechanism by which CNNs operate on signals.
Semantic segmentation is implemented by applying patch processing densely across the image.
The concept describes the evolution of feature maps as they pass through successive layers of a network.
Downsampling is the specific mechanism mentioned that reduces spatial resolution in deeper layers.
Adversarial examples are specifically discussed as a method to identify weaknesses in the learned representations of neural network architectures.
The primary pedagogical motivation for pooling is to convert the translation equivariance of convolutional layers into translation invariance.
Channelwise pooling is an extension of the pooling concept applied across the channel dimension rather than spatial dimensions.
The sliding filter interpretation relies on the mapping between output locations and input receptive fields.
Spatial outputs are achieved by ensuring the final layer of the CNN remains a high-resolution feature map.
Producing spatial maps requires limiting the amount of downsampling performed by the network.
The conceptual shift to image-to-image architectures relies on the technical ability of CNNs to produce spatially varying outputs.
The suitability of CNNs for images is predicated on the formal definition of translation invariance.
The concept discusses the enduring relevance of principles derived specifically from the CNN architecture.
Locality is identified as one of the two core principles (local processing) that remain ubiquitous in sensory processing.
The text explicitly defines the local principle as processing each patch identically and independently.
The concept highlights the integration of global information across patches as a fundamental stage in modern architectures.
Encoders in CNNs are typically constructed using layers that downsample the image into a lower-dimensional feature map.
A decoder is defined as the synthesis network that performs the inverse operation of an encoder.
Decoders function by upsampling low-dimensional features layer by layer to reconstruct an image.
The information bottleneck is the low-dimensional representation produced by the encoder before it is passed to the decoder.
The bottleneck exists as a constrained transmission point between the encoder and the decoder.
A U-Net is specifically defined as an encoder-decoder architecture augmented with mirrored skip connections.
Residual Networks are deep architectures characterized by their extensive use of skip connections between blocks.
Cascading involves composing multiple layers of dilated convolutions with increasing dilation rates.
SVD is used to decompose general filters into a sum of separable filters.
One implementation of upsampling layers involves dilating the signal (inserting zeros) before convolving.
Receptive fields are introduced as an important concept specifically for working with CNNs.
This concept explains the mechanism by which the size of receptive fields increases through the layers of a network.
Downsampling layers are identified as a key factor that multiplies the receptive field size.

overlay.rationale: The ability to produce pixel-wise labels demonstrates the image-to-image mapping power of CNNs.
The emergence of semantic heatmaps in deep layers is the functional basis for semantic segmentation tasks.
Pooling layers are defined as a specific type of downsampling layer that summarizes patches using aggregate statistics.
Global pooling is a specialized form of pooling that aggregates over the entire spatial extent of a feature map.
An FCN is a specific type of CNN that lacks fully connected layers.
The sliding filter concept describes the functional behavior of an FCN.
The sliding filter mechanism is what enables CNNs to function as image-to-image architectures.
To maintain spatial resolution for prediction maps, global pooling layers (which collapse spatial dimensions) must be removed.
This concept generalizes the view of CNNs from simple image classifiers to general-purpose domain-to-domain mapping architectures.
CNNs provide a concrete implementation of the locality principle by splitting image interpretation into small patch-based problems.
U-Nets maintain the benefits of an information bottleneck while using skip connections to preserve high-frequency spatial detail.
A residual connection is a specific type of skip connection used within ResNet blocks to additively perturb the input.
Dilated convolution spaces out the filter elements themselves, whereas strided convolution spaces out the application points.
Low-rank filters are a broad category of filters parameterized by few weights, of which dilated filters are a specific example.
Separable filters are a common type of low-rank filter formed by the outer product of 1D kernels.
Downsampling layers reduce spatial dimensions, with strided convolution serving as a primary example.
Upsampling layers perform the inverse spatial transformation of downsampling layers.
The growth of receptive fields allows deeper layers to aggregate information from larger regions, enabling more abstract features.
